newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania tourism sector eyes fast privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Romania tourism sector eyes fast privatisation.

text.p: Romania's tourism industry, in the doldrums for several years due to slow reforms, will undergo radical reforms and fast privatisation in a bid to relaunch the sector, a senior official said on Friday.
"We want to privatise fast," Tourism Minister Akos Birtalan told a political and economic conference of the Swiss-based Crans Montana Forum, held in Bucharest.
The four-day conference, which ends on Sunday, has drawn hundreds of businessmen and politicians from the European Community, the United States and Canada to Bucharest.
Birtalan said those "paying the best price under the most advantageous circumstances" would be the successful bidders in the tenders planned by his ministry to privatise the sector.
The ministry has already issued a plan to revive Romania's tourism, he said.
The project is part of a tough reform package planned by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's new centrist government.

In January, Birtalan ordered the liberalisation of hotel tariffs as part of moves to put the sector on a free market footing. The decision put an end to communist-era practices to apply different tariffs to locals and foreigners.
"Our data show real privatisation so far amounts to about 4.2 percent. This is unacceptably low," Birtalan said.

Romania has good tourism potential. Its holiday spots are endowed with some of the least spoiled scenic alpine pistes or beaches in Europe. But, at a time when tourism to ex-communist states like Hungary and the Czech Republic is growing, Romanian tourism is declining mainly due to concerns about quality.

Small accommodation providers such as bed-and-breakfasts or guest houses are rare and lack financial suppport. The country is running a travel deficit as Romanians travelling abroad are more numerous than foreigners visiting Romania.

Birtalan blamed the situation on the former leftist government, ousted in elections last November, which he said had failed to implement radical reforms and had delayed real privatisation in tourism by using substitutes which included partial management-buyouts or long-term rental contracts.
Run-down hotels and restaurants are a common sight across Romania following the reluctancy of their administrators to upgrade services or invest in assets they do not own.
"Such arrangements will be replaced by leasing contracts whose legal and economic aim will be to achieve ownership," Birtalan said.
The Crans Montana Forum is a Swiss foundation set up in 1989 to promote international dialogue amid the changes caused by the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe.
